doc.title: Danny Barker Interview (Louis Armstrong memorial broadcast), 1971-07-09

title: Danny Barker on his guitar playing and wish to be a writer
summary: The host asks Barker about himself; he talks about playing rhythm guitar in New York bands and being a frustrated writer.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: The woods stood still on Blueberry Hill And it wasn't until my dream come true Down when the willows played Love's sweet melody And all of those vows we made Were never to be Though we were born You followed me still Oh, you were my thrill On Blueberry Hill Come find your hill with me, baby We'll see what we will see I'll bring my heart with me I'll be with you where the fairies are blue Yes, each afternoon we'll go Yes, I've been a moon real good You are winning and you will go Yes, I've been a moon real good Doing the willows played Love's sweet melody And all of these vows we made, baby Were never to be Don't be one part Yes, you better be still For you were my thrill Get Blueberry Hill Yeah Now let me tell you, Danny, tell me something about yourself

Because I think the people I think we ought to know something about you Your instrument Has your instrument always been the guitar Yes, I play guitar You know, play a little There's so much to learn about a guitar You know, and I start playing rhythm and bands and and getting in New York There's so many great guitar players if you want to jump in competition and try to I never aspired to be the greatest, you know, just went along and played And what would be your goal? What kind of goal have you established for yourself in this? Oh, well, no, I'm a frustrated writer I always wanted to write from a kid Oh, write music? No, write Just write literature Yeah, but I never had time and time and really steady, you know, to learn But I'm a frustrated writer Oh, that's how you're now Writers are gifted with a kind of type of sensitivity of observation And you have really observed Louis Yes, well, you know, and he observed When you write, you know, you observe what's happening in the world, too You know, you have to read to write So you're already reading all kinds of stuff So it makes you have a different insight of what's happening in the world And a lot of things other people get annoyed by It don't even affect me because it was a reason I knew the reason Well, I think you should be the person who might And this might be the beginning of your having something very authentic to say about Louis Particularly from someone I'm not capable enough of saying nothing about Louis Except for that And nobody, nobody Very few people are capable of being Going into depth to understand Louis The honest thing you can do with Louis Is grab up his records and enjoy his music And if you see a movie, go and see him Not the stereo things, stereotype things he did in the movie But go see the man acting alive Right, right there You see, before I was trying to figure out Louis, you can't figure out Louis There's only one Armstrong There was only one Caruso There was only one Einstein One Thomas Edison One Henry Ford I put him above all those people too Because when all the machines and gimmicks they made You know, Armstrong was the music will be gone You know, like His, his, his, his He had a natural prowess He had a natural combination of things going for him That he took advantage of apparently Just natural Because he certainly didn't get it out of any books in school He just done with what he done What he done was an earthy youngster from New Orleans That had seen New Orleans, lived New Orleans And he had happy days in New Orleans, rough days in New Orleans And first opportunity he
